The deliberate misplacing, exploitation or wrongful temporary or permanent use of a resident's belongings or money, including medications.
A bound or controlled record that shows the quantity of each resident's controlled substance on hand, each dose removed, and each count by two staff members. It is a facility-chosen control.
Comparing the count on hand to the count log and the medication administration record to make sure every dose is accounted for.

procedures: Only the staff authorized under HLT-02 may administer medication. Staff who are not authorized may only remind, hand over, open containers or physically assist residents who self-administer (OAC 3701-16-09(E)-(H)). Staff never fill pill organizers for residents.

All prescription medications, including controlled substances, are kept in locked storage. Controlled substances are kept in a separate locked compartment inside the locked medication area (a facility-chosen control). Medications are never left on counters, carts or in rooms unattended.

Keys or codes to medication storage are held only by the nurse or authorized medication staff on duty. The key holder signs a key log at the start and end of each shift. Keys are never shared, copied or left in a lock. Lost keys are reported to the Administrator immediately and the lock is changed.

When a controlled substance is delivered, two staff members (the nurse or medication staff and a second staff member) open the package, compare each item with the pharmacy label and the prescriber's order, count it, and both sign the count log. Any difference is reported to the pharmacy and Administrator the same day.
Medications are not repackaged or relabeled by the facility. Each resident's controlled substance stays in the pharmacy-labeled container (OAC 3701-16-09(H)-(I)).

Count log control: at every shift change, the outgoing and incoming medication staff count together every controlled substance in the facility's custody, compare the counts with the count log, and both sign. A count log page is kept for each resident and drug.

Each dose removed is recorded on the count log and the medication administration record at the time of administration, with date, time, dose and signature. If a dose is refused, dropped or wasted, a second staff member witnesses the waste and signs the record.

If a count does not match, the two staff members recount, review the administration record and check for waste or error. If the difference is not resolved before the outgoing staff member leaves, the nurse calls the Administrator immediately. The outgoing staff member stays until the Administrator or nurse directs otherwise.

Any unresolved discrepancy, missing controlled substance or sign of tampering is treated as a possible theft. The Administrator starts an investigation the same day, records it in the incident log (SAF-02), notifies the pharmacy and prescriber, and notifies law enforcement and any licensing or regulatory body whose notice is required by law.

Suspected diversion or misappropriation of a resident's medication is handled as possible exploitation under SAF-01. The Administrator reports it to the agencies named in SAF-01 and cooperates with investigators. The resident, sponsor and physician are told of any effect on the resident's treatment.

Staff suspected of diversion are removed from medication duties immediately while the matter is investigated. Staff may be asked to cooperate with drug testing as permitted by facility policy and law. Any staff member who is found to have diverted medication is terminated and reported as required by law.

Residents who self-administer controlled substances keep them in locked storage in their room, as set out in the service plan and HLT-01, and staff check that the supply matches the label at least monthly if the resident agrees.

When a resident leaves, dies or a medication is discontinued, controlled substances are sent with the resident, or destroyed with the written consent of the resident or representative, by two staff witnesses, and recorded on the medication record and count log (OAC 3701-16-09(H)-(I); see HLT-01 and HLT-09).

The Administrator or nurse audits controlled-substance records at least monthly. The audit compares a sample of count logs, administration records, pharmacy deliveries, and the amounts on hand, and looks for patterns by shift or staff member. Findings go to the quality committee (GOV-04).

Hiring controls: no one with a disqualifying offense or a registry finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation is hired for direct care (see STF-02). Staff receive training on this policy at orientation and at least annually (STF-03), including how to recognize diversion and how to report it.
Staff may report concerns to the Administrator, to the nurse, or directly to the regulatory agencies. [AGENCY NAME] will not retaliate against anyone who reports in good faith.

At the annual policy review, the Administrator confirms the paragraph letter of this checklist item in the current full text of OAC 3701-16-09 and updates this policy if the rule has changed (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is carried out, controls key access, investigates discrepancies, reports suspected diversion, and confirms the rule paragraph reference at each review.
Administers controlled substances on a prescriber's order, performs and signs shift counts, receives deliveries with a second staff member, and reports discrepancies right away.

responsibilities.role: Medication staff and direct care staff
responsibilities.duty: Perform only the tasks they are authorized to do, serve as second counter or witness when asked, and report any concern about missing medication.
Assists with reconciliation, reviews records on request and is notified of discrepancies.

documentation: Controlled-substance count log by resident and drug, with two signatures at every shift change
Medication administration record
Key log for medication storage
Delivery and receipt record with two signatures
Waste, refusal and destruction records with witness signatures
Incident log entries and investigation file for any discrepancy
Monthly audit results and quality committee minutes
Training records on this policy

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, the Administrator and the governing body
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect and financial exploitation, to screen out staff who are not eligible to work in direct care, and to make sure every allegation is reported, investigated and addressed without reprisal.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to be free from abuse and from financial exploitation (ORC 3721.13(A)(1)-(24) and (A)(25)-(29)). [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, misappropriation and exploitation of any resident. The facility does not hire for direct care anyone with a disqualifying offense under ORC 3721.121(C)(1), anyone who fails the required forms or fingerprinting, or anyone with an abuse, neglect or misappropriation finding on the Ohio or another state's nurse aide registry or a license action for the same (OAC 3701-16-06(L)). Residents may voice grievances to staff, ODH or others of their choice without reprisal (ORC 3721.13(A)(34)-(35)). Staff who suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation report to county adult protective services, law enforcement and ODH as Ohio law requires. The Administrator will have legal counsel confirm the current statutory reporting duties and contact details, as the specific reporting statute is not cited in this manual. [AGENCY NAME] does not retaliate against any resident or staff member who reports, and investigates every allegation. Residents' funds and property are protected under OAC 3701-16-11(B)-(C).

definitions.definition: Any willful infliction of injury, unreasonable confinement, intimidation, punishment or sexual contact, whether physical, verbal, sexual or emotional, that causes or could cause harm, pain or mental anguish.
Failure to provide the goods and services needed to avoid physical harm, mental anguish or illness, including failure to supervise, feed, give medication or respond to a call for help.
The unlawful or improper use of a resident's money, property, medications or resources, including coercing a resident to assign assets or take on obligations, for someone else's benefit.
Information that would lead a reasonable person to believe abuse, neglect or exploitation may have occurred. Staff do not need proof before reporting.
Any adverse action such as threats, discharge, discipline, a change in care or a change in treatment taken because someone reported or complained in good faith.

procedures: Hiring screens: before a person is offered direct-care work, the Administrator completes the forms, fingerprinting and criminal records check, and checks the Ohio nurse aide registry and other states' registries as required (see STF-02). No one is hired for direct care who has a disqualifying offense under ORC 3721.121(C)(1), who fails to complete the forms or fingerprinting, or who has a registry finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation or a related license action (OAC 3701-16-06(L)).

Prevention training: every employee completes training on resident rights, abuse, neglect and exploitation, reporting duties, dementia communication and de-escalation at orientation, before working alone with residents, and at least annually (see STF-03). Volunteers and contractors who may have contact with residents are given the same rules.

Staff may never accept a gift, loan or a role as a resident's guardian or attorney-in-fact, and may not manage a resident's funds, unless a related person or the resident gives witnessed written authorization as required by OAC 3701-16-11(B)-(C) (see RR-05 and STF-06).

The Administrator posts the residents' rights and the phone numbers for reporting, the state long-term care ombudsman and ODH where residents and visitors can see them. Residents and sponsors are told at admission how to report a concern (see RR-01, RR-02, RR-03).

Duty to report: any employee, contractor or volunteer who sees, hears of or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation must immediately protect the resident from further harm and report it to the Administrator or, if the Administrator is involved or unavailable, to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]'s designee or the governing body. Staff may also report directly to the agencies. They do not need the Administrator's permission, and they must not wait to do so.

Immediate protection: staff separate the resident and the alleged person, obtain medical care if needed, and call 911 for any serious injury or crime. The alleged staff person is removed from all resident contact immediately, pending the investigation. Evidence is preserved and the area is not cleaned until it is safe to do so.

External report: the Administrator immediately reports every suspected case to county adult protective services at [APS PHONE], to local law enforcement at [LAW ENFORCEMENT PHONE] when a crime may have occurred, and to ODH at [PHONE]. Where Ohio law requires a written report, the Administrator submits it on the form and within the time required. The report is made by telephone first. The Administrator records the date, time, person contacted and report number.

Notification: the Administrator promptly notifies the resident's sponsor, physician and, for waiver residents, the case manager. A significant health change resulting from an incident is also notified to the sponsor within 12 hours as required by ORC 3721.13(A)(34)-(35).

Investigation: the Administrator, or a person not involved in the allegation, starts an investigation immediately, and in any case on the same day. It includes interviews of the resident, witnesses and staff, review of schedules, records and any video, and a written conclusion. The investigation is completed within 5 working days, and any later update is added if an outside agency's investigation is still open.

Protective action: the Administrator makes any change needed to protect residents, such as changing assignments, retraining, discipline, termination, or referral to a licensing board or the nurse aide registry. A substantiated allegation against an employee results in termination unless the Administrator and governing body document a different, lawful outcome.

Resident follow-up: the nurse assesses the resident, and the care plan is updated if needed (see ADM-05). The resident is offered counseling or other support, and access to the ombudsman and a residents' rights advocate is arranged (see RR-03).

Financial protection: the Administrator makes sure that resident funds held are accounted for as required by OAC 3701-16-11(B)-(C) and ORC 3721.13(A)(25)-(29), including itemized monthly bills, quarterly accounting if funds are delegated, a separate interest-bearing account for funds over $1,000, a surety bond and a final accounting. No one may pressure a resident to give up assets or sign over property.

No retaliation: [AGENCY NAME] does not retaliate against any resident or employee who reports or cooperates. Residents who complain are not moved, restricted or treated differently. Any retaliation by a staff member is cause for discipline up to termination. The Administrator checks in with the reporting resident or staff member at 30 days to confirm there has been no reprisal.
Every incident is also entered in the incident log (see SAF-02). Reports about missing or diverted medications follow HLT-10.

Legal counsel reviews the Ohio reporting duties, statutory citations and agency contact details at least once a year, and whenever the law changes. The Administrator updates this policy and the posted contact list within 30 days of any change (see GOV-03).
Every year the Administrator reviews all allegations and outcomes, identifies trends and reports to the governing body and quality committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, receives reports of allegations and outcomes, and investigates any allegation involving the Administrator.
Screens staff, makes external reports, directs investigations, protects residents and ensures no retaliation.
Protect residents, report immediately any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, preserve evidence and cooperate with investigators.
Assesses and treats the resident after an allegation, documents injuries and updates the care plan.
Safeguard resident funds, provide required accountings and report any suspected financial exploitation.

documentation: Background check, fingerprint and registry results for every direct-care hire
Training records on abuse, neglect, exploitation and reporting
Report log with date, time, agency, person contacted and report number
Investigation file with interviews, evidence and written conclusion
Incident log entry and notifications to the sponsor, physician and case manager
Corrective action and disciplinary records
Annual review of allegations and trends
Legal counsel's annual review of reporting duties and contacts

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, the nurse on duty, the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident or accident involving a resident is investigated, recorded in a separate incident log that the director can access, and noted in the resident record, so that the facility responds promptly and prevents repeat events.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] investigates and documents each incident. This policy meets the checklist item B, Incident handling, of OAC 3701-16-12(B). The facility keeps an incident log separate from the resident record that is accessible to the director of ODH. The log shows the time, place and date, a general description of the incident, and the care provided or action taken. A notation is also made in the resident's record. On a significant adverse change in a resident's health status, the facility also provides immediate intervention, notes it in the record, gives information to the treating party, and notifies the sponsor (OAC 3701-16-12(A); see HLT-04). This rule item is a requirement that the policies must address and is carried out through this policy.

definitions.definition: Any unusual event that harms or could harm a resident, such as a fall, injury, medication error, elopement, resident-to-resident altercation, suspected abuse or neglect, missing property, fire, or other event affecting resident health or safety.
A single running log, kept separate from the resident records, listing each incident with time, place, date, general description and the care provided or action taken.
The Director of the Ohio Department of Health, or the Director's designee, such as a surveyor, who may ask to see the incident log.

procedures: Any staff member who sees or learns about an incident first makes sure the resident is safe, calls 911 for any emergency, and calls the nurse on duty or on call right away.

The nurse, or if none is on site the senior staff member, checks the resident, gives or arranges needed care, and records the actions taken. The resident's physician is notified as needed under HLT-04.

Before the end of the shift, the staff member who saw or found out about the incident completes the incident report form. It states the date, time and exact place, who was involved, a factual description, witnesses, injuries and the care provided or action taken. Opinions and blame are not recorded.

The staff member or nurse writes a notation in the resident's record that the incident occurred and what care was given, with the date and time. The record notation refers to the incident but does not replace the log entry.

The staff member or nurse enters the incident in the incident log, which is kept apart from the resident record, in a form that the Administrator controls. Each entry shows the time, place and date, a general description, and the care provided or action taken.

The staff member or nurse notifies the Administrator immediately for a serious incident (injury needing treatment, hospital transfer, suspected abuse or neglect, elopement, fire, death) and otherwise by the start of the next business day.

The Administrator starts an investigation within one business day (immediately for serious incidents). The investigation includes statements from staff and witnesses, review of the area and equipment, review of the resident's care plan and a determination of the cause.

The sponsor is notified of significant incidents and of any significant adverse change in health status in line with HLT-04. The resident's physician and, for waiver residents, the case manager are informed as appropriate.

External reports: the Administrator determines whether the incident must also be reported elsewhere. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01. A missing resident follows SAF-03. A fire, or an injury, illness or death caused by fire or smoke, is reported under SAF-09 within 24 hours. A death follows HLT-09. Medication or controlled-substance losses follow HLT-10.

The Administrator documents the investigation findings and the action taken, such as care plan changes, equipment repair, retraining or discipline, on the incident report. The nurse updates the service plan where needed (see ADM-05).

The incident log is kept in a secure place, separate from the resident records, and is made available to the director on request, including during inspections. The Administrator checks that it is complete at least monthly.

At least monthly, the Administrator reviews the log for trends by resident, time, place, staff and type of incident. Findings, such as repeated falls, are reported to the quality committee under GOV-04 and used to update fall prevention, supervision and staff training.
Incident logs and reports are retained for the period required in REC-01. Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (see STF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Protect the resident, call for help, report incidents the same shift, and complete the incident report and record notation accurately.
Assesses the resident, provides or arranges care, notifies the physician and sponsor, and updates the care plan.
Keeps the separate incident log accessible to the director, investigates every incident, makes external reports and reviews trends.
Reviews incident trends and decides on preventive actions (see GOV-04).

documentation: Incident log, kept separate from resident records, with time, place, date, description and care or action taken
Incident report form with statements and investigation findings
Notation in the resident's record
Notification records for the physician, sponsor and other agencies
Monthly trend review and quality committee minutes

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff, nurses and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To prevent residents from leaving the building unsafely or without supervision, and to make sure staff locate a missing resident quickly and notify local law enforcement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has written procedures for locating missing residents, including notifying local law enforcement. This policy meets checklist item J(3), Disaster plan: procedures for locating missing residents, including notifying local law enforcement, of OAC 3701-16-13(J)(3). These procedures are part of the written disaster preparedness plan required by OAC 3701-16-13(J), which is kept on site and electronically off-site (see SAF-05). Elopement risk is assessed at admission and at each reassessment. A resident is never locked in a room or physically restrained to prevent elopement. Secured special care units may be used only as permitted by OAC 3701-16-09(L): the placement must be individualized, reviewed at each reassessment, code compliant and not based solely on a diagnosis (see HLT-05 and SAF-04). Every elopement or missing-resident event is logged as an incident.

definitions.definition: A resident whose whereabouts are not known and who cannot be found in the building or grounds after a first check, or who is outside without staff knowledge when they need supervision.
A resident leaving the building or grounds without the knowledge of staff, or without supervision they need for safety.
A finding from assessment that a resident has a history of wandering or leaving, cognitive impairment or exit-seeking behavior that makes unsupervised departure likely and unsafe.

procedures: Risk assessment: the nurse or Administrator screens each resident for elopement risk at pre-admission (ADM-01), at admission and at every reassessment (ADM-04), and after any change of condition or near-miss. The result is written in the assessment and service plan.

For each resident at risk, the service plan states supervision level, interventions (such as check frequency, door alarms or wearable alert devices, structured activities), and what staff do if the resident tries to leave. A current photo and physical description are kept in the front office file with the sponsor's consent.
Door alarms or alert systems are tested weekly and the test is logged. The maintenance staff repairs any failure the same day and the Administrator arranges extra supervision until it is repaired.

The Administrator posts this procedure at the nurses' station and trains all staff at orientation and annually. At least one missing-resident drill is held each year on every shift (see SAF-05 and SAF-06).

Discovery: any staff member who finds a resident missing, or is told so, shouts or radios a missing-resident alert, names the resident and gives a description. The nearest staff member keeps watch on the exits and the remaining residents are kept safe.

Initial search: the charge nurse or senior staff member directs staff to check the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, dining room, outdoor areas, parking lot, nearby roads and any other likely place, using the photo and description. Time started is written down at once.

Calling law enforcement: if the resident is not found in the first check, which must not exceed 15 minutes, staff call 911 or the local law enforcement agency at [LAW ENFORCEMENT PHONE]. For a resident at high risk, or one who has left in unsafe weather or who has a medical need, staff call immediately without waiting for the search to finish. Staff give the name, description, clothing, time last seen, medical or cognitive condition and photo.

The charge nurse notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee notifies the sponsor and the resident's physician as soon as possible. The Administrator tells the waiver case manager the same day when the resident is on the Assisted Living Waiver.

The search continues, in cooperation with law enforcement, until the resident is found. A staff member stays by the phone and keeps a written timeline of the search. If staffing falls short for resident safety during the search, the Administrator calls in additional staff.

When the resident is found, the nurse assesses the resident right away for injury, dehydration, hypothermia or other harm, arranges medical care and tells law enforcement, the sponsor and the physician that the resident has been found.

Within 24 hours the Administrator completes the incident report and log entry (SAF-02), reviews how the resident left, and fixes the cause, for example a door alarm, staffing, supervision or an unsafe exit. If the incident involved neglect, the Administrator follows SAF-01.

The nurse reassesses the resident within 72 hours and updates the service plan (ADM-05). If risk cannot be managed with the services the facility may lawfully provide, the Administrator starts the process in ADM-06. A secured unit may be used only if the conditions in OAC 3701-16-09(L) are met, and the use is reviewed at each reassessment.

Staff never lock a resident in a room or use restraints to prevent elopement (see SAF-04). A resident who is able to make decisions retains the right to go out. For such residents, the facility uses the sign-out procedure in the resident agreement and the service plan and respects the resident's choices.
The Administrator reviews all missing-resident events and drills at least quarterly in the quality committee and makes a written record of improvements (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this procedure as part of the disaster plan, notifies the sponsor and authorities, investigates each event and trains staff.

responsibilities.role: Charge nurse or senior staff member
responsibilities.duty: Directs the search, calls law enforcement, assesses the resident when found and keeps the timeline.
Know which residents are at risk, respond to alarms, report a missing resident immediately and take part in the search.
Test and repair door alarms and exits and record the tests.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment and service plan interventions
Resident photo and description file
Door alarm test log
Search timeline with times of discovery, law enforcement call and recovery
Incident report and incident log entry
Notification records for the sponsor, physician, case manager and law enforcement
Drill records and training records
Quality committee review

policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff, nurses, the Administrator, and contracted providers who work in the facility
policies.purpose: To make sure that no resident is restrained, secluded or otherwise restricted in a way that is not allowed, to protect resident rights and dignity, and to teach staff safer alternatives.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical, chemical or isolation restraints. OAC 3701-16-09(L) forbids them, including locked room doors and geriatric chairs. Residents have the right to be free from restraint under ORC 3721.13(A)(1)-(24). That statute addresses restraint only on physician order with a 12-hour emergency limit, but because this facility is licensed as a residential care facility under OAC 3701-16-09(L), [AGENCY NAME] does not use that pathway. In an emergency, staff call 911. Secured special care units are allowed only if the placement is individualized, reviewed at each reassessment, code compliant and not based solely on diagnosis (see HLT-05). The facility does not admit or retain a resident who needs restraint. Because the facility serves residents under the Assisted Living Waiver, it also meets the home and community-based settings requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c), under which any restriction on a resident's rights must be individually justified, documented and agreed to (see GOV-07).

definitions.definition: Any method, device or equipment that the resident cannot easily remove and that limits free movement or normal access to the body, including belts, vests, wrist ties, tucked sheets, lap trays or geriatric chairs the resident cannot get out of, and holding a resident down.
A drug or dose used to control behavior or restrict movement for staff convenience or discipline, and not to treat a medical condition.
Confining a resident alone in a room or area, including locking a room door or blocking the door so the resident cannot leave.
A unit with secured exits for residents with dementia, permitted only under the conditions in OAC 3701-16-09(L) and HLT-05.
Any measure that limits a resident's freedom of movement, choices or rights, such as limits on access to food, visitors, personal belongings or the community.

procedures: No staff member may apply, order or use a physical, chemical or isolation restraint on any resident. No resident room door is ever locked from the outside, and no resident is kept in a geriatric chair, with a lap tray or in a bed, or any other device, that the resident cannot remove.

Devices such as bed rails, wheelchair belts and trays are used only if they are assessed and ordered, do not prevent the resident from freely getting out of bed or the chair, and can be removed by the resident. The nurse assesses these devices at admission and every reassessment. A device that prevents free movement is treated as a restraint and is removed.

Medications are never used to sedate or control a resident for staff convenience or discipline. The nurse reviews any new psychotropic medication order with the prescriber and records the diagnosis, target symptoms and monitoring (see HLT-01 and HLT-02).

Admission screening: during pre-admission screening and assessment (ADM-01 and ADM-04), the nurse checks whether a person's needs would require restraint or isolation. A person who needs restraint is not admitted, and a resident who develops this need is processed under ADM-06 and ADM-07.

Alternatives: staff first use less restrictive approaches, such as redirecting, calm communication, meeting unmet needs (pain, toileting, hunger, boredom), changing the environment, structured activity, one-to-one attention, and consulting the physician for medical causes (see HLT-05 and DL-02).

Emergencies: if a resident is a danger to self or others, staff keep a safe distance, remove others, use verbal de-escalation, call the nurse and the Administrator, and call 911 if the danger cannot be reduced. Staff do not restrain the resident. They may use only the minimum non-restraining measures needed to protect from immediate harm, and these are documented.

Secured special care unit: a resident may be placed in a secured unit only on the basis of an individualized assessment, not solely on a diagnosis. The need, less restrictive options tried, and the sponsor's or resident's agreement are recorded in the service plan. Placement is reviewed at each reassessment and whenever the resident's condition changes, and the unit must comply with building and fire codes (OAC 3701-16-09(L); see HLT-05).

HCBS settings: any restriction on a resident's rights or choices, including limits on visitors, access to food or movement, is allowed only if the assessed need is documented in the person-centered service plan, less intrusive methods were tried, the resident or sponsor consents in writing, and it is reviewed regularly, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c) and GOV-07. A restriction applied to all residents for staff convenience is not allowed.

Training: all staff are trained at orientation, before working alone, and at least annually on the prohibition on restraints, on recognizing disguised restraints, on de-escalation and on alternatives (see STF-03). Training is recorded.

Reporting: any staff member who sees or suspects a restraint or seclusion must report it immediately to the nurse or Administrator, and the resident is released at once if restrained. The Administrator investigates, records the event in the incident log (SAF-02), reports it as abuse where required under SAF-01, and takes corrective and disciplinary action.
Notification: the Administrator tells the sponsor and physician of any restraint event, the injury if any, and the corrective action taken.

Review: the Administrator reviews, at least quarterly, the use of devices, psychotropic medications, secured-unit placements and any restraint events, and reports to the quality committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that no restraint is used, approves any secured-unit placement, investigates any report and trains staff.
Assesses devices and medications, identifies alternatives, reviews secured-unit placement at each reassessment and documents the person-centered plan.
Never restrain or isolate a resident, use alternatives and report any concerns immediately.
Adopts this policy and reviews quarterly reports on restrictive practices.

documentation: Assessment and reassessment notes on devices, behavior and secured-unit need
Service plan entries on alternatives and any documented restriction with consent
Medication reviews for psychotropic drugs
Training records on restraints and alternatives
Incident log entries and investigation files for any event
Quarterly review and quality committee minutes

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
policies.applies_to: All residents, staff, volunteers and visitors at [AGENCY NAME], [ADDRESS]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can protect residents and respond in a fire, severe weather, a nearby hazard or any other emergency, and can evacuate every resident, including residents with impaired mobility, to a predetermined appropriate facility.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] maintains a written disaster preparedness plan to be followed in an emergency or disaster. The plan is readily available in the facility and is also kept electronically so it can be reached off site. This policy meets OAC 3701-16-13(J) (item J). The plan includes each of the following.

(1) Evacuation (item J(1), OAC 3701-16-13(J)(1)(a)-(b)). The plan has procedures for evacuating all individuals. It makes provisions for residents with impaired mobility (item J(1)(a)). It also makes provisions for transporting all residents to a predetermined appropriate facility or facilities (item J(1)(b)).

(2) Fire (item J(2), OAC 3701-16-13(J)(2)). The plan protects all persons in a fire and sets out fire control and evacuation procedures. It includes a fire watch. It requires prompt notice to the local fire authority and the State Fire Marshal whenever fire detection, alarm or sprinkler systems are impaired or inoperable. Detailed fire procedures and drills are in SAF-06.

(3) Severe weather (item J(4), OAC 3701-16-13(J)(4)). The plan has procedures for residents' health and safety in severe weather such as tornadoes and floods. It designates tornado shelter areas.

(4) Nearby hazards (item J(5), OAC 3701-16-13(J)(5)). If the facility is near an area with specific disaster potential, such as an airport, chemical plant or railroad tracks, the plan includes procedures for that hazard. The Administrator documents the hazard assessment even when the answer is that no such hazard applies.

(5) Notice to ODH (item J(6), OAC 3701-16-13(J)(6)). The Administrator notifies the ODH director by email or phone when normal business services are interrupted by an emergency or disaster involving the facility.

The plan also addresses missing residents, including notice to law enforcement (see SAF-03). Building egress, exit and fire-protection features are maintained as required by OAC 3701-16-13 (C39) so the plan can be carried out.

definitions.definition: An event such as fire, tornado, flood, utility failure, hazardous material release or other emergency that threatens resident safety or interrupts normal operations.
A resident's limited ability to move out of the building or to shelter without help, for example because of a wheelchair, walker, bed confinement, cognitive impairment or an injury.
A predetermined facility that has agreed to take residents when the building must be evacuated and that can meet their needs (see SAF-09).
Continuous, documented patrol of the building by trained staff when fire detection, alarm or sprinkler systems are impaired or inoperable.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) is responsible for the written disaster plan. The Administrator reviews it at least annually and after every drill or actual event that exposes a gap, and records the review date on the plan.

The Administrator keeps one complete paper copy of the plan at [LOCATION, e.g., the nurse/med station and the Administrator's office] where any staff member can reach it on every shift. A complete electronic copy is stored in [SECURE CLOUD OR OFF-SITE LOCATION] and the Administrator and [BACKUP STAFF TITLE] have access credentials.
Each time the plan is revised, the Administrator updates both the paper and electronic copies the same day and removes superseded paper copies from the unit.

The Administrator maintains a current evacuation list for every resident showing mobility level, devices used, cognitive status, oxygen or other equipment, and the number of staff needed to move the resident. The list is updated within 24 hours of any change in a resident's mobility and reviewed monthly.

The plan names the predetermined receiving facility or facilities and lists their address, phone number and contact person. Written transfer agreements are kept under SAF-09. The Administrator confirms the contact information at least annually.

The plan lists the transport method for each category of resident: ambulatory, wheelchair, and non-ambulatory. It identifies the vehicles or transport providers that will be used ([TRANSPORT PROVIDER/VEHICLES]) and how medications, records, equipment and resident identification will travel with residents.
In a fire, staff follow the fire procedures in SAF-06: rescue, alarm, contain, evacuate. The person in charge calls 911 and keeps residents at a safe assembly point under head-count.

If the fire detection, alarm or sprinkler system is impaired or inoperable, the person in charge immediately notifies the Administrator, the local fire authority and the State Fire Marshal, and starts a fire watch. Staff patrol all areas of the building at least every 30 minutes, or more often if the fire authority directs, and record each round in the fire watch log. The fire watch continues until the system is restored and the Administrator documents the restoration.

The plan designates tornado shelter areas by location, and floor plans and signage show them. During a tornado warning the person in charge moves residents to the shelter areas, giving priority to those with impaired mobility, takes a head-count, and keeps residents away from windows until the all-clear is received.

For flood or other severe weather, the person in charge monitors weather alerts, moves residents to safe areas as the plan directs, secures medications and records, and decides with the Administrator whether to shelter in place or evacuate.

The Administrator completes and documents a hazard assessment of the surrounding area (airports, chemical plants, railroad tracks and similar). If any hazard exists, the plan includes specific shelter-in-place or evacuation steps for it. If none exists, the assessment says so.

When an emergency or disaster interrupts normal business services at the facility, the Administrator or the person in charge notifies the ODH director by email or phone, using the Bureau of Regulatory Operations (Licensure Unit) at (614) 466-7713 or liccert@odh.ohio.gov, or any other contact ODH designates. The notice is made as soon as safety allows, and the date, time, person notified and method are recorded.
When a resident is missing, staff follow SAF-03, which includes notifying law enforcement.

After an evacuation, relocation or sheltering event, the Administrator notifies each resident's representative and physician, accounts for every resident, and documents where each resident was sent. Resident relocation and any return to the building are coordinated under HLT-04 and GOV-06 where applicable.

Within 7 days after any actual event or drill, the Administrator holds a debrief with staff, identifies what failed, assigns corrective actions with due dates, and records them on the drill/event evaluation form (see SAF-06).
All new staff are oriented to the plan under SAF-06 within 3 working days of hire, and the plan is covered again in annual staff training.

responsibilities.duty: Owns and annually reviews the plan; keeps paper and electronic copies; notifies ODH of business interruptions; assigns and tracks corrective actions.
Initiates the plan, calls 911 and the Administrator, directs staff, takes head-counts and starts a fire watch when systems are impaired.
Know their roles, shelter and evacuation routes, and resident evacuation needs; take part in drills and training.
Keeps egress routes, fire and safety systems and emergency equipment in working order and reports impairments immediately.

documentation: Written disaster preparedness plan (paper copy on site and electronic copy off site) with review/revision dates
Resident evacuation list and mobility roster
Receiving facility list and transfer agreements (SAF-09)
Hazard assessment of nearby disaster potential
Fire watch logs and records of notice to the local fire authority and State Fire Marshal
Record of notice to ODH of business interruption
Drill and event evaluations and corrective action records (SAF-06)

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: All residents, all staff on every shift, volunteers and visitors at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect all persons in a fire through working fire protection systems, trained staff and residents, posted evacuation plans, and drills that are evaluated and recorded.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] maintains a fire safety and evacuation program that meets OAC 3701-16-13, as follows.

Fire plan (item J(2), OAC 3701-16-13(J)(2)). The facility has a plan for protecting all persons in a fire and procedures for fire control and evacuation. It includes a fire watch and prompt notice to the local fire authority and the State Fire Marshal when fire detection, alarm or sprinkler systems are impaired or inoperable (see SAF-05 for the fire watch procedure).

Drills and records (items K-M, OAC 3701-16-13(K), (L), (M)). The facility conducts 12 fire drills a year, with one on each shift every 3 months. Each staff member takes part in at least one fire drill a year. Residents are evacuated in at least 2 drills per shift each year. The facility conducts 2 disaster drills a year, and one is a tornado drill held between March and July. Problems found are investigated and corrected. A written drill record and evaluation is kept for 3 years.

Floor plans (item N, OAC 3701-16-13(N)). A wall-specific floor plan is posted on each section or floor.

Staff fire and evacuation training (item P, OAC 3701-16-13(P)). All staff are trained in fire control and evacuation procedures within 3 working days of hire. No staff member is alone with residents before this training is completed.

Annual fire prevention training (item Q, OAC 3701-16-13(Q)). Regularly scheduled staff on all shifts receive fire prevention training every year, and records are kept.

Resident training (item R, OAC 3701-16-13(R)). All residents are trained in the proper actions to take in a fire, tornado, disaster or other emergency.

The facility also keeps automatic sprinklers and fire alarms in working order with records, performs a monthly fire safety inspection kept for 3 years, maintains carbon monoxide detectors, and keeps egress clear. Door hold-open devices are used only if they release on power loss or fire alarm (C42, C39).

definitions.definition: A practice of the fire alarm response and exit procedure, conducted on a specific shift and recorded in writing.
A fire drill in which residents actually move to the exit or assembly point, not only staff.
A floor plan mounted on the wall and oriented to show the viewer's location ("you are here").
A day the new staff member is scheduled to work. Training must be completed within 3 of these days of hire.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) names a Fire Safety Coordinator ([NAME/TITLE]) who schedules drills, runs monthly inspections and keeps records. The Administrator reviews the records every month.

Fire drill schedule: the Coordinator prepares an annual calendar of 12 fire drills so that every shift (day, evening, night) has one drill in every 3-month period. Drill times are varied and not announced to residents in advance.

Resident evacuation: the calendar designates at least 2 drills per shift each year in which residents are actually evacuated to the assembly point. For residents who cannot be safely moved, the drill evaluation records the evacuation method and time that was simulated or used.

Staff participation: the Coordinator checks the drill rosters to make sure every staff member, including part-time and PRN staff, takes part in at least one fire drill each year. Staff who miss a drill take part in the next one scheduled for their shift.
Disaster drills: the Coordinator schedules 2 disaster drills a year. One is a tornado drill held between March and July. The other covers another hazard from the disaster plan (SAF-05).

Conducting a drill: the Coordinator or a designee starts the drill, observes staff response, and times activation of the alarm, staff reporting, door closing, resident evacuation, head-count and all-clear. The shift person in charge manages the response.

Written record: immediately after each drill, the observer completes a drill record showing date, time, shift, drill type, the number of residents evacuated, staff who took part, time to complete evacuation, problems found and the evaluation.

Investigation and correction: any problem, such as alarm failure, blocked exit, slow evacuation or a staff member who did not know their role, is investigated. The Administrator assigns a corrective action and due date on the drill record and signs it off when corrected. A repeat drill is held when the problem was significant.
Retention: drill records and evaluations are kept for 3 years in the [LOCATION] fire safety binder and are available to ODH and fire inspectors.

Floor plans: the Coordinator ensures a wall-specific floor plan is posted on each section or floor. Each plan shows room use, alarm sending stations, evacuation routes and exits, fire alarms and extinguishers, and the flow of resident evacuation. Plans are updated within 5 working days of any change to the layout, room use or equipment and checked monthly.

New-staff training: before any new staff member is scheduled alone with residents, the Coordinator or a trained designee covers fire control and evacuation procedures, alarm and extinguisher locations, exits, resident evacuation needs and the disaster plan. The training must be done within 3 working days of hire, and the new staff member signs and dates the record.

Annual fire prevention training: each year the Coordinator trains regularly scheduled staff on all shifts in fire prevention (for example, causes of fire, oxygen and smoking safety, electrical safety, extinguisher use, and keeping exits clear). Attendance is recorded, and staff who miss a session are trained within 30 days.

Resident training: within [7] days of move-in and again at least annually, staff train each resident, in a way the resident can understand, in the proper actions to take in a fire, tornado, disaster or other emergency. Residents with cognitive impairment receive repeated simple instructions and staff-directed evacuation. Attendance is recorded.

Monthly fire safety inspection: each month the Coordinator inspects exits and egress routes, extinguishers, alarm panels, emergency lighting, hold-open devices, electrical cords and appliances, and carbon monoxide detectors. The inspection is recorded and kept for 3 years.

Systems: the Administrator contracts with a qualified vendor to maintain the automatic sprinkler system and fire alarm system and keeps service and inspection records. The Coordinator checks that the vendor's records are current.

Impaired systems: if a fire alarm, detection or sprinkler system is impaired or inoperable, staff start a fire watch and notify the local fire authority and State Fire Marshal promptly, as directed in SAF-05. The Administrator documents the date, time, persons notified and restoration date.

Egress: staff keep exits and corridors free of obstructions at all times. Hold-open devices on doors are used only if they release on power loss or fire alarm. Any violation found is corrected immediately.
After a real fire, the Administrator follows SAF-09 for the 24-hour report to the State Fire Marshal and ODH.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the program is funded and carried out; reviews records monthly; signs off corrective actions.
Schedules and runs drills; keeps records; conducts monthly inspections; keeps floor plans current; delivers or arranges training.
Directs the response to drills and real alarms; takes head-counts; reports problems.
Complete training; take part in drills; know exits, alarms and extinguisher locations; keep egress clear.

documentation: Annual fire and disaster drill calendar
Written drill records and evaluations (kept 3 years), with corrective action sign-off
Posted wall-specific floor plans (copy kept on file) and change log
New-staff fire and evacuation training records, showing completion within 3 working days of hire
Annual fire prevention training records for all shifts
Resident emergency training records
Monthly fire safety inspection records (kept 3 years)
Sprinkler and fire alarm inspection and service records
Fire watch logs and notices to fire authorities (when systems are impaired)

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All residents, staff, volunteers and visitors at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To provide a safe, sanitary and comfortable environment and to prevent, detect and control the spread of infections and communicable disease among residents and staff.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] has a written infection prevention and control program that meets OAC 3701-16-12(C) (item C). The program contains written policies and procedures to assure a safe, sanitary and comfortable environment and to control the development and transmission of infections and diseases. It monitors compliance with those policies, investigates and controls infections, and trains all staff.

Item C(1), OAC 3701-16-12(C)(1). The Administrator designates one or more infection prevention and control designees. The designee's name and contact information, including email, are submitted on the ODH-prescribed electronic system within 10 days of appointment and within 10 days of any change.

Item C(2), OAC 3701-16-12(C)(2). The facility has a tuberculosis (TB) control plan that meets the standards of OAC 3701-15-03.

Item C(3), OAC 3701-16-12(C)(3). The facility has a written surveillance plan for monitoring and tracking infections using nationally recognized criteria, such as McGeer, with a data collection tool and a process for using the data.

The program also covers isolation, hand hygiene, laundry rules and a legionella water management program (C38). Staff health requirements follow OAC 3701-16-06(A)-(C) (C13): staff with a transmissible disease may not work while the disease is communicable unless their duties are modified, staff may not work impaired by alcohol or drugs, and every paid worker has a health examination within 30 days before starting or on the first day, with a copy retained. Staff with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials are covered by the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030.

definitions.definition: The trained staff member(s) designated by the Administrator to carry out the infection control program.
Ongoing collection, tracking and review of infections among residents (and staff where relevant) using standard definitions to identify trends and outbreaks.
A nationally recognized set of surveillance definitions for infections in long-term care settings.
Basic infection prevention practices applied to all residents at all times, including hand hygiene, glove use and safe handling of blood, body fluids and sharps.
A written program to reduce the risk of Legionella growth and spread in the building's water systems.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) appoints at least one infection prevention and control designee ([NAME/TITLE]) who has completed the training the Administrator has judged appropriate for the role, and records the appointment in writing.

Within 10 days of appointment, or of any change in designee, the Administrator submits the designee's name and contact information (including email) on the ODH-prescribed electronic system and keeps a copy of the confirmation.

The designee maintains the written infection prevention and control program, including policies on standard precautions, hand hygiene, isolation, cleaning and disinfection, laundry, sharps and waste handling, and food safety, and reviews it at least annually.

Hand hygiene: staff wash hands or use alcohol-based hand rub before and after resident contact, before handling food or medications, after using the toilet and after removing gloves. Soap, water, hand rub and gloves are kept stocked in care areas and the designee audits hand hygiene practice at least quarterly.

Isolation: when a resident has a known or suspected communicable infection, the designee and the resident's physician or other authorized provider decide on precautions (for example, room restriction, contact or droplet precautions). Staff post the approved precaution signage, supply the required protective equipment and tell the resident and representative. Precautions are lifted only when the designee confirms the criteria are met.
Laundry: staff handle soiled linen and clothing with gloves, bag it at the point of use, wash it according to the laundry procedure in DL-03, and keep clean and soiled items separate.

Surveillance: the designee uses a written surveillance plan based on nationally recognized criteria, such as McGeer. Each new infection is logged on the facility's data collection tool, with resident, date, site, symptoms, culture or treatment, and room or unit. The designee reviews the log monthly for trends and clusters.

Use of surveillance data: the designee reports findings monthly to the Administrator and quarterly to the QA committee (GOV-04). When rates rise or a cluster is found, the designee investigates, sets control measures, and records them and their results.

TB control plan: the facility follows its written TB control plan, which meets the standards of OAC 3701-15-03. The plan covers staff TB screening (see STF-04), resident screening at admission (see ADM-01), and actions when active TB is suspected. The designee reviews it annually.

Employee health: no staff member with a transmissible disease works while it is communicable unless duties are modified to prevent transmission. Staff report symptoms to their supervisor before the shift and the Administrator decides on exclusion or modified duties and documents the decision. Staff may not work impaired by alcohol or drugs.
Pre-employment exam: each paid worker has a health exam within 30 days before starting work or on day one. The Administrator retains a copy in the personnel record (STF-04, STF-05).

Bloodborne pathogens: the Administrator provides an exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030 for staff with occupational exposure. It includes training, protective equipment, sharps safety, post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, and hepatitis B vaccine offered as that standard requires.

Legionella water management: the Administrator maintains a written water management program. It identifies water systems, controls such as temperature and flushing of unused outlets, monitoring and corrective actions. The maintenance designee carries out and logs those tasks as the program specifies.

Outbreaks: when the designee suspects an outbreak (for example, several residents or staff with the same illness), the designee tells the Administrator at once, starts the control measures and arranges required notification to the local health department and others as required by law (see REC-02).

Training: all staff are trained in the infection control program at orientation and at least annually (STF-03). Training covers hand hygiene, standard precautions, isolation, laundry and symptoms staff must report. Attendance is recorded.
Residents and visitors: staff give residents and visitors guidance on hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette and may restrict visits from people with active symptoms in line with RR-01 and SAF-08.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints designee; submits designee information to ODH within 10 days; provides resources; reviews surveillance reports; ensures TB plan and water management program are in place.
Runs the program and surveillance; investigates infections and outbreaks; audits practices; trains staff.
Follow standard precautions and isolation orders; report their own symptoms and resident infections promptly.
Carries out and logs water management tasks.

documentation: Written infection prevention and control program with annual review date
Designee appointment record and ODH electronic submission confirmation
TB control plan meeting OAC 3701-15-03
Written surveillance plan, infection log/data collection tool and monthly trend reviews
Isolation precaution records
Employee health exams and exclusion/modified-duty records
Bloodborne pathogens exposure control plan and training records
Legionella water management program and monitoring logs
Staff infection control training records

policies.title: Smoking, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: All residents, staff, visitors, volunteers and animals at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect residents from fire and smoke hazards, to honor residents' right to receive visitors on their own schedule, and to allow animals safely.
policies.policy:
Smoking policy (items F(2) and U). This policy is the facility's smoking policy that is given to residents before admission under OAC 3701-16-07(F)(2) (item F(2)), and it carries out the smoking requirements of OAC 3701-16-13(U) (item U; C43). The current rule text places the smoking requirements at 3701-16-13(U), and this policy follows that text. Smoking and vaping are permitted only in designated areas. No smoking or flame is permitted where oxygen is stored or used, and "No smoking" signs are posted in those areas. The facility takes reasonable precautions for residents who smoke, uses non-combustible ash receptacles and provides shelter in bad weather for residents who smoke outdoors.

Visitors. Residents may receive visitors of their choosing at any time, and may control their own schedule and access to visitors, consistent with the HCBS settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c) for Assisted Living Waiver residents. Any limit on visitors is applied only for a documented, resident-specific safety reason, is supported by the resident's assessment and service plan, and is reviewed regularly (see GOV-07).

Pets. The facility has a written pet protocol developed after consultation with a veterinarian, as required by OAC 3701-16-11 (C35).

definitions.definition: An area identified in writing by the Administrator where smoking and vaping are permitted, away from oxygen storage or use and from building air intakes.
Any room or space where oxygen is stored or used, including resident rooms where oxygen is in use.
Any person who visits a resident, including family, friends, clergy, advocates, the Ombudsman, and agency representatives.
A domestic animal that lives with, or regularly visits, a resident or the facility, other than a service animal.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) identifies and documents the designated smoking and vaping area(s), indoors or outdoors, and posts them on the floor plan. Smoking and vaping are not allowed anywhere else on the premises.
Before admission, staff give each prospective resident and representative the smoking policy in the pre-admission packet (ADM-02) and explain it. Staff record in the admission file that it was given.

At admission and at each reassessment, staff ask about smoking and vaping and record each resident's status. Residents who smoke are assessed for safe smoking, including cognitive ability, mobility, use of oxygen and ability to handle smoking materials, and the result goes into the service plan (ADM-04, ADM-05).

Where a resident needs supervision to smoke safely, the service plan says what is required. Staff keep lighters and matches for that resident where the plan requires it and supervise smoking as the plan states.

The maintenance designee supplies non-combustible ash receptacles in each designated area, empties them at least daily into a metal container kept outside the building, and checks the area for hazards during the monthly fire safety inspection (SAF-06).
Staff ensure a sheltered smoking area or other reasonable protection is available in bad weather, and that residents who need help get there and back safely.

Oxygen: staff post "No smoking" signs at each location where oxygen is stored or used, including entrances to rooms where oxygen is in use. Staff do not allow smoking or open flame (candles, incense, lighters) in these areas.
When a resident starts oxygen, staff inform the resident, roommates and visitors of the no-smoking rule, post signs the same day, and review the rule in the service plan.
If staff see smoking or flame near oxygen, or smoking outside designated areas, they stop it immediately, make the area safe, tell the Administrator and complete an incident report (SAF-02).

Visitors: the Administrator publishes the facility's visiting arrangements, which allow visits at hours the resident chooses. The front desk or staff on duty may set reasonable security steps such as visitor sign-in, but these do not restrict a resident's access to visitors without a documented reason.

Restrictions: a limit on visitors for a particular resident is used only if it is supported by a specific assessed need, is documented in the service plan with the less intrusive methods tried, has the resident's informed consent, and is reviewed regularly. The Administrator approves every such limit, and it is a resident-specific modification under GOV-07.
Visitors with symptoms of communicable illness may be asked to wait, wear a mask or visit another way, under SAF-07. Staff explain the reason to the resident and visitor.

Pet protocol: the Administrator consults a veterinarian to write the facility's pet protocol, which covers the types of animals allowed, vaccination and health requirements, care and sanitation responsibilities, areas where animals may and may not go, and handling of resident allergies or fear of animals. The consult is recorded with date and veterinarian name.

Before a resident's pet moves in or a visiting animal program starts, staff check proof of health and vaccination required by the protocol, confirm no roommate objection or allergy, and document approval and the resident's care responsibilities.
The Administrator reviews the smoking policy, visitor arrangements and pet protocol at least annually and after any related incident.

responsibilities.duty: Designates smoking areas; approves visitor restrictions; develops the pet protocol with a veterinarian; reviews policies annually.
Give the smoking policy and visitor and pet information to prospective residents before admission and record it.
Assess and supervise smoking per the service plan; post and enforce oxygen signage; report violations.
Provides and maintains ash receptacles and signage; checks smoking areas monthly.

documentation: Smoking policy and record that it was given before admission (ADM-02)
Designated smoking area list and floor plan marking
Resident smoking assessments and service plan entries
"No smoking" oxygen signage check (monthly inspection record)
Visitor restriction approvals, assessed need, consent and review notes (if any)
Pet protocol with veterinarian consultation record
Pet health/vaccination and approval records
Incident reports (SAF-02)

policies.title: Fire Reporting and Transfer Agreements
policies.applies_to: Administrator, person in charge on every shift, and all staff at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every fire is reported on time to the State Fire Marshal and ODH, and that residents can be moved to another facility able to meet their needs when conditions at [AGENCY NAME] threaten their health or safety.
policies.policy:
Fire reporting (item W, OAC 3701-16-13(W)). [AGENCY NAME] reports any fire, fire damage, or illness, injury or death from fire or smoke inhalation to the State Fire Marshal and the Ohio Department of Health within 24 hours, using the forms prescribed by each agency.

Transfer agreements (item X, OAC 3701-16-13(X)). The facility keeps written transfer agreements with other facilities that can meet the needs of residents who must be transferred because their health or safety is, or may be, adversely affected by conditions in the facility. Agreements are reviewed annually and copies are kept on file.

definitions.definition: Any fire, any fire damage to the building or contents, and any illness, injury or death caused by fire or smoke inhalation, regardless of size or whether the fire department responded.
A written agreement with another facility to accept residents who must be transferred because conditions at [AGENCY NAME] adversely affect, or may adversely affect, their health or safety.
A facility with a transfer agreement that can meet the needs of the residents being moved.

procedures: When a fire occurs, staff first protect residents following SAF-06 and the disaster plan (SAF-05) and call 911. Reporting steps begin only after residents are safe.
The person in charge notifies the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) as soon as safety allows, giving what happened, where, injuries and the response.

The Administrator determines whether the event is reportable. Any fire, even if put out by staff and with no fire department response, is treated as reportable if it caused damage, or illness, injury or death from fire or smoke inhalation. When in doubt the Administrator reports.

The Administrator, or a designee in the Administrator's absence, obtains the current report forms from the State Fire Marshal and ODH and keeps blank copies on file so they are available on every shift.

The Administrator completes and sends the report to the State Fire Marshal and to ODH within 24 hours of the event, using each agency's own form. ODH Licensure Unit contact: (614) 466-7713, liccert@odh.ohio.gov. The Administrator records the date, time, method and person who sent each report and keeps proof of transmission.
The Administrator also completes an incident report (SAF-02) and notifies the affected residents' representatives and physicians (HLT-04). If a resident dies, HLT-09 is followed.
If a fire involves impairment of the alarm, detection or sprinkler system, the Administrator also follows the fire watch and notice steps in SAF-05 and SAF-06.
Within 7 days, the Administrator reviews the event with staff, identifies causes, assigns corrective actions and records them. Findings go to the QA committee (GOV-04).

Transfer agreements: the Administrator identifies facilities in the area, such as other licensed residential care facilities, assisted living or nursing facilities, that can meet the needs of the facility's residents. Those with different levels of care, including memory care if the facility serves residents with dementia, are included.

The Administrator negotiates a written transfer agreement with each facility. It states the facility's contact person and phone number, the circumstances in which residents would be transferred, how resident records and medications will be sent and the transport arrangements. Both parties sign and date it.

The Administrator reviews each agreement at least once a year to confirm it is still valid and contact details are current, and notes the review date and reviewer on the agreement. An agreement that is no longer valid is replaced promptly.
Copies of all current agreements are kept on file at [LOCATION] and are given to ODH on request. The receiving facilities named in the disaster plan (SAF-05) match those in the agreements.

If conditions at the facility threaten residents' health or safety (for example, loss of heat, water or electricity, or fire damage), the Administrator decides, with input from physicians and, where relevant, the fire authority, whether to transfer residents. The Administrator activates the transfer agreements, tells residents and representatives, and sends records and medications with each resident.
The Administrator records each transfer under these agreements, including who was moved, where, when and why, and tells ODH as required under SAF-05 and REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Determines reportability; files 24-hour reports with the State Fire Marshal and ODH; negotiates, signs and reviews transfer agreements annually; directs any transfer.
Ensures resident safety, calls 911 and the Administrator, and preserves information for the report.
Makes the 24-hour report and activates the agreements when the Administrator is not available.

documentation: Copies of fire reports sent to the State Fire Marshal and ODH, with transmission proof showing the 24-hour timeframe
Incident report and corrective action record
Written transfer agreements, with annual review dates
Record of any resident transfers made under the agreements
Blank copies of the State Fire Marshal and ODH report forms

policies.title: Food Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: All residents and all dietary, care and supervisory staff at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive the meals, snacks and drinking water the facility has agreed to provide, planned in advance, kept on hand in adequate supply, and, where a resident needs a therapeutic diet, supervised by a dietitian.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides dietary services under OAC 3701-16-10 (C34). The facility states in each resident agreement the number of meals it offers each day, from zero to three. Meals offered are [NUMBER, 0-3] per day. No more than 16 hours pass between supper and breakfast, and an evening snack is offered. Menus are planned a week in advance and kept for 3 months. The facility keeps a week of staple foods and 2 days of perishable foods on hand. Drinking water is always available to residents. Therapeutic diets are supervised by a dietitian, and staff who prepare or serve them are trained by the dietitian first (OAC 3701-16-06(E)-(G), C16).

definitions.definition: A diet ordered for a resident to treat a medical condition or to manage a condition through nutrition, for example a diabetic, low-sodium, renal or texture-modified diet.
A registered or licensed dietitian engaged by the facility to supervise therapeutic diets and train staff.
Non-perishable foods such as canned goods, dry goods, cereals and shelf-stable items that can sustain residents when deliveries are interrupted.
Foods that need refrigeration or freezing, such as milk, produce, meat and eggs.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) decides the number of meals the facility offers daily (0 to 3). The number and the meal times are written in the resident agreement (RR-04) and the pre-admission packet (ADM-02).

The meal schedule is set so that no more than 16 hours elapse between the evening meal and breakfast. The dietary supervisor ([NAME/TITLE]) checks the schedule each time meal times change and records the actual supper and breakfast times.
Staff offer an evening snack to every resident each night, and record what was offered. Residents who miss supper are offered a replacement meal or extra snack.

The dietary supervisor plans menus at least a week in advance, posts them where residents can see them, and offers choices or substitutes of similar nutritional value. Residents' food preferences and cultural or religious needs are considered.
When a menu changes, the dietary supervisor writes the substitution on the posted menu or on a substitution record. Menus as planned and as served are kept for 3 months from the date of service.

The dietary supervisor keeps a supply of staple foods sufficient for a week and perishable foods sufficient for 2 days, based on the current number of residents. A written inventory is checked weekly, and any shortage is replaced promptly.

Drinking water is always available. Staff keep water pitchers, dispensers or water fountains in common areas stocked and clean, offer fluids to residents at each meal, snack and medication pass, and take extra steps for residents who cannot get water themselves.

Therapeutic diets: before a resident is started on a therapeutic diet, staff obtain the diet order from the resident's authorized prescriber and record it in the service plan (ADM-05). The Administrator or designee refers the resident's diet to the dietitian.

The dietitian reviews the diet order, develops or approves the diet plan and menus for it, and supervises how it is carried out. The dietitian's name, credentials and contact information are kept on file.

Dietitian training: before any staff member prepares or serves a therapeutic diet, the dietitian trains that person on the diet, including what is allowed and not allowed, portion and texture requirements and how to check meals. Training date, content and attendees are recorded and filed in the personnel record (STF-03, STF-05).

Care staff and dietary staff check each therapeutic-diet meal against the diet card or tray ticket before serving. Any error or refusal is reported to the dietary supervisor, and a recurring problem is reported to the dietitian and the resident's prescriber.

Staff observe residents for changes in eating, weight, swallowing or hydration and report them to the person in charge. The person in charge follows HLT-04 for changes of condition. Significant weight loss or poor intake is also reported to the dietitian for review.

The dietitian reviews each resident on a therapeutic diet as often as the diet order or service plan requires, and at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., every 6 months], and records the review. The service plan is updated as the diet changes (ADM-04, ADM-05).
Food safety and sanitation: staff follow the food handling, hand hygiene and cleaning procedures in SAF-07 and DL-03. Staff with symptoms of a communicable illness do not prepare or serve food.

Emergency supplies: the dietary supervisor makes sure the staples and water on hand also meet the needs described in the disaster plan (SAF-05) and updates the supply list when the resident count or diets change.
The Administrator reviews menus, inventory records and diet records at least quarterly and reports findings to the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Sets the number of meals offered; ensures resources, staff and a dietitian are available; reviews records quarterly.
Plans and posts menus; keeps menu records 3 months; maintains the week of staples and 2 days of perishables; makes sure the evening snack and meal-interval rule are met.
Supervises therapeutic diets; trains staff before they prepare or serve them; reviews residents on diets.
Offer meals, snacks and water; check diet cards; report changes in intake or condition.

documentation: Resident agreement stating meals offered (RR-04)
Posted menus and substitution records, kept 3 months
Meal schedule and evening snack records showing the 16-hour limit was met
Weekly food inventory (staples and perishables)
Therapeutic diet orders, dietitian approvals and review notes
Dietitian training records for staff before therapeutic diets
Water availability checks

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: Administrator, activity coordinator, all personal care staff, volunteers and all residents
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has access to varied activities and to information about the wider community, and that the people who plan activities are trained for the residents they serve.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges varied activities for residents and offers a daily newspaper or community brochures. It also gives residents information about community activities and how to get to them, as required by OAC 3701-16-11(A). Anyone who plans activities is trained for the cognitive impairment and mental illness populations the facility serves, as required by OAC 3701-16-06(D). Participation is voluntary. Residents are never required to take part in an activity, and residents are never used in place of staff (see STF-01). The program reflects each resident's assessed interests, abilities and cultural background, and it is adapted for residents with cognitive impairment.

definitions.definition: The staff member or members assigned by the Administrator to plan, schedule and lead or arrange activities.
Printed or electronic listings of local events, senior centers, libraries, faith communities and other community resources, offered when a daily newspaper is not provided.
Residents with cognitive impairment or serious mental illness, for whom activity planners must have specific training.

procedures: The Administrator designates, in writing, one or more activity planners and keeps their names in the staffing schedule. The Administrator confirms that each planner has completed the cognitive impairment and serious mental illness training described in STF-03 before the planner independently designs programming.

At admission and at each reassessment (ADM-04), the planner or a designee records the resident's interests, past routines, abilities, sensory needs, language and cultural or faith preferences, and the resident's preferences for group versus individual activities. This information goes in the resident's service plan (ADM-05).

The planner prepares a written activity calendar at least monthly. It includes a mix of physical, social, creative, cognitive, spiritual and community-based options. It also includes some options for residents who stay in their rooms or who cannot join group activities.

The calendar is posted in a common area and in large print. Copies are given to residents on request and to families or representatives who ask. Staff read the calendar to residents who cannot read it.
